extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of advertising/history; historians of early-modern British lotteries and commerce
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards, practices, and normative arrangements used in early-modern English lotteries and their advertising (licensing, drawing methods, publicity, accounting, agents, and legal conditions). Focused account of 16th–17th century British lottery practice as recorded in a history of advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal letters-patent / licence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Lotteries were to be established under letters-patent or special licence from the Crown (e.g., grants 'for thirteen years to come, all lotteries whatsoever invented or to be invented' to certain officers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters-patent created a legal monopoly and formal permission; patentees could be granted power to issue licences and name agents. Government notices explicitly prevented drawing of any lotteries except those under his Majesty's letters-patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public, supervised drawing for transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings were often required/expected to be public and supervised (e.g., 'in his Majesty's Presence', blanks to be told over, papers rolled up in his Presence, a child appointed to draw the prizes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royal presence, appointed drawers, and public counting of blanks were presented as means to guarantee 'Equity and Fairness' and to restore public confidence after cheating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed particulars/appraisement of prizes must be provided
rubrics_metrics.description: A printed Particular of the Appraisement, with divisions into lots, 'will be delivered gratis' by the agent/promoter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promoters should make printed appraisals and lists of lots available free to potential adventurers so purchasers can assess prize values before investing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refund policy if lottery not drawn by specified date
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoters sometimes promised that 'each Adventurer shall receive their Money back if the said Lottery be not drawn and finished before' a specified date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deadline-for-drawing clause was used to protect purchasers and as an advertising assurance to induce trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display of prizes for daily visual inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices were maintained 'where the several Volumes or Prizes may be daily seen' so adventurers could view prizes 'by which visual Speculation [they] understand their real Worth better than by the Ear or printed Paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping a public office/showroom where prizes can be inspected was promoted as a transparency and sales strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification of total number of lots and blanks (odds transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotions specified 'The whole Number of the Lots' and the 'Number of the Blanks as above ordered', with full enumeration of lots and blanks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing exact counts of lots and blanks and their distribution was used to show the scheme's structure and calculate receipts vs prizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent appraisal and valuation of prizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prizes (notably jewels) were 'particularly valued and appraised by' named reputable jewellers and valuers, producing a total valuation (e.g. 'amounting to Twenty Thousand Pounds').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of recognized appraisers added credibility to the stated prize values and to the fairness of the sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent/banker liability and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoters appointed a responsible person (e.g., 'Mr. Francis Child...will be answerable for their several adventures') to receive monies and guarantee payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a reputable banker or agent personally answerable for adventurers' monies was an assurance device and early form of escrow/banking responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government prohibition on unlicensed lotteries
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices in the Gazette forbade the drawing of any lotteries 'except those under his Majesty's letters-patent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal prohibition limited lawful promotion to patentees and was used to suppress fraudulent or competing schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustees/farmers and management structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees/trustees could farm counties or contract for management of lotteries, and trustees commissioned by Letters Patent managed the patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal management bodies (trustees) and farming-of-counties arrangements institutionalized the marketing and administration of lotteries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline and registration of purchasers' names/inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adventurers were 'desired to bring or send in their Monies, with their Names, or what other Inscription or Motto ... by the ninth of May' so the Author could put up lots and inscriptions into boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring names/inscriptions by a deadline enabled organizers to prepare the physical lots and maintain traceability of tickets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promoter attestations and obligations to deliver prizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoters (e.g., Ogilby) declared and attested that prizes drawn were delivered, addressing complaints that winners had not received prizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly attesting prior fulfillment and keeping an office for delivery were ways to combat accusations of fraud and to promote trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of promotional narratives and testimonial stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoters and advertisers circulated 'wonderful' winner-stories and superstitious tales (boy's penny becomes £1000) to stimulate sales; popular tracts satirized such methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Storytelling, lucky-chance narratives, and spectacle were routine advertising techniques to increase ticket purchases; critics warned these exploited public credulity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear ticket pricing and prize-schedule proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotions set out explicit propositions: e.g., 'put in five Shillings shall draw a Lot', 'put in twenty-five Shillings ...', and enumerated prize packages and their values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing explicit price tiers and corresponding prize guarantees (or compensatory small prizes) was central to selling tickets and to purchasers' evaluation of expected value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent supervision and drawing methods (glasses, superintendents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some schemes were 'drawn with the lots out of two glasses, superintended by John Lilly and Edward Barrel, Esqs., Mr Deputy Collins, and Mr William Proctor, stationer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of procedural devices (glasses, named superintendents) was another mechanism to demonstrate fairness and reduce accusations of manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary accounting: receipts versus declared prize values
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotions and reports compared 'The whole Mass of Books ... amounting ... to thirteen thousand seven hundred Pounds' against 'Total received is but four thousand, one hundred, and ten Pounds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and critics monitored and advertised the arithmetic of total receipts, prize values, and ticket counts to show either generosity or to reveal commercial calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions attached to charitable distributions from lottery proceeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Charitable gifts arising from lotteries (e.g., Reading) could carry strict conditions: the 40l fund to be lent to six poor tradesmen for five years gratis, with conditions that recipients not keep an inn or tavern and must reside in the borough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lottery proceeds used for public/charitable ends were often bound by detailed conditional trusts governing use, security, and eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous and scheduled drawing operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some large lotteries were 'commenced ... and continued day and night until' a given date; others 'continued in Drawing day and night for the space of two or three dayes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large schemes required extended drawing schedules and public venues (St Paul's, theatres) to complete all lots, implying logistical requirements for promoters and expectations for the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to notify drawing and offices via Gazette/advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing dates and arrangements were to be 'notified in the Gazette' and advertisements named specific offices and persons where monies were to be paid and tickets obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official Gazette notices and frequent advertisements told prospective purchasers where/when to pay and see prizes — an essential part of lawful and effective promotion.
